questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This tests practical CKAD pattern: file-driven config synchronization, idempotent object creation, secret management, and namespace-scoped network policy.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer tooling, kubectl in-cluster, ConfigMap/Secret management, TLS sidecar, NetworkPolicy scoping.
- Cadence-based reconciliation and minimal YAML skeletons for CKAD.

## Code Example
```javascript
# Minimal skeleton for a Deployment that performs config sync
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: config-sync
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: config-sync
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-tools
          image: alpine:3.17
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache jq curl kubectl"]
      containers:
        - name: main
          image: my-registry/config-sync:latest
          env:
            - name: SYNC_INTERVAL
              value: "300s"
      volumes:
        - name: config
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: config-pvc
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /health
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 10
        periodSeconds: 5
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /health
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 30
        periodSeconds: 10
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you secure the TLS sidecar and rotate certs without restarting pods?
- How would you test reconciliation and conflict resolution between file changes and cluster objects?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to compose common CKAD primitives into a cohesive, maintainable per-namespace app: InitContainer logic, ConfigMap-driven behavior, TLS handling, and network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- InitContainer installs rendering tool and pre-processes inputs
- ConfigMap and Secret drive runtime config and secrets
- Sidecar for TLS rotation and secret refresh
- Readiness/Liveness probes for quick failure detection
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricts egress to internal endpoints

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: docs-portal
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: docs-portal
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: docs-portal
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: docs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: docs-pvc
        - name: tls-cert
          secret:
            secretName: docs-tls
      initContainers:
        - name: render-md
          image: pandoc/pandoc:latest
          command: ["sh", "-c", "cp -r /docs/* /rendered/; pandoc -f markdown -t html /docs/*.md -o /rendered/index.html"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: docs
              mountPath: /docs
            - name: rendered
              mountPath: /rendered
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:stable
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          volumeMounts:
            - name: rendered
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle new Markdown files added at runtime?
- How would you scale this per-namespace deployment with multiple replicas?

## Why This Is Asked

apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: rbac-audit
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: restricted-sa
      initContainers:

"```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design a safe, observable canary rollout using standard Kubernetes resources and NGINX Ingress without a service mesh.

## Key Concepts
- Canary deployment pattern with separate Deployments
- Ingress annotations (nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary, canary-weight)
- Progressive traffic shifting and rollback strategy
- Observability: latency, error rate, saturation

## Code Example
```yaml
# Stable Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: frontend
  namespace: prod
  labels:
    app: frontend
    version: stable
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: frontend
      version: stable
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: frontend
        version: stable
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: frontend
        image: frontend:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```
```yaml
# Canary Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: frontend-canary
  namespace: prod
  labels:
    app: frontend
    version: canary
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: frontend
      version: canary
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: frontend
        version: canary
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: frontend
        image: frontend:1.2-canary
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```
```yaml
# Ingress (production path)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: frontend-ingress
  namespace: prod
  annotations:
    # enable canary routing for the canary backend
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "10"
spec:
  rules:
  - host: "frontend.example.com"
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: frontend-canary
            port:
              number: 80
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you promote canary to 50% and then 100% safely?
- What metrics would you monitor to decide progression or rollback?
- How would you rollback if the canary fails without affecting stable users?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question validates understanding of per-namespace resource governance in Kubernetes. It tests knowledge of how LimitRange and ResourceQuota work together to control pod sizing and cluster resource allocation.

## Key Concepts
- **LimitRange**: Sets default requests/limits applied to Pods that don't specify resources
- **ResourceQuota**: Enforces hard limits on total namespace resource consumption
- **Policy alignment**: Ensuring Deployments specify resources matching namespace defaults
- **Verification**: Testing policy enforcement with intentional over-allocation
- **Rollback**: Strategy for removing or scaling back resources when policies need adjustment

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: analytics-lr
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    default:
      cpu: "200m"
      memory: 256Mi
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: "100m"
      memory: 128Mi
```
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: analytics-quo
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  hard:
    cpu: "400m"
    memory: 512Mi
    requests.storage: "1Gi"
```
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: reporter
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: reporter
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "200m"
            memory: "256Mi"
```
## Verification Commands
```bash
kubectl apply -f limitrange.yaml
kubectl apply -f quota.yaml
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl describe resourcequota analytics-quo -n analytics
kubectl run overload-test --image=busybox --restart=Never --requests=cpu=500m,memory=600Mi --dry-run=server
```
## Rollback Strategy
```bash
kubectl delete -f quota.yaml
kubectl delete -f limitrange.yaml
kubectl scale deployment reporter --replicas=0 -n analytics
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to orchestrate time-based batch workloads, integrate ConfigMaps and Secrets with PVs, and enforce idempotence and rollback for Kubernetes workload automation.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob with Job template and parallelism
- ConfigMap mounted as /etc/reconcile
- PVC mounted at /data/reconcile
- Secret-provided DB credentials via env vars
- Resource requests/limits and graceful termination
- checksum/config annotation to trigger updates
- RBAC: RoleBinding for service account

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: reconcile-cron
  namespace: data-warehouse
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        metadata:
          annotations:
            checksum/config: "abcdef1234" # placeholder hash
        spec:
          serviceAccountName: reconcile-sa
          containers:
          - name: reconciler
            image: my-registry/reconcile:latest
            envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: db-creds
            volumeMounts:
            - name: reconcile-rules
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Question Matters for CKAD

This question validates mastery of **production-grade Kubernetes patterns** — not just textbook syntax. It combines seven CKAD concepts (CronJob, Job, InitContainer, ConfigMap, Secret, PVC, NetworkPolicy) in a realistic multi-tenant operational scenario.

## Key Concepts Tested

| Concept | Role in Pipeline |
|---------|-----------------|
| **CronJob** | Schedules periodic migrations with concurrency control |
| **Job** | Executes single migration attempt (created by CronJob) |
| **InitContainer** | Prepares SQL client before main container runs |
| **ConfigMap** | Versioned, injectable migration scripts without image rebuilds |
| **Secret** | Secure credential injection with namespace isolation |
| **PVC** | Persistent log storage for debugging and audit trail |
| **NetworkPolicy** | Enforces zero-trust network per namespace |

## Critical Design Decisions

1. **Why InitContainer for SQL client?**
   - Keeps main image minimal (security) and migration image separate from app image
   - Trade-off: adds startup latency and complexity

2. **Why PVC at /logs?**
   - Jobs are ephemeral; logs would be lost without persistence
   - Enables audit trail and post-mortem debugging

3. **Why NetworkPolicy egress restriction?**
   - Tenant database should only receive connections from migration Jobs
   - Prevents lateral movement in case of pod compromise

4. **Why probes on Job Pod?**
   - Liveness: ensures stuck jobs are restarted (but can cause issues with long migrations)
   - Readiness: typically irrelevant for Jobs, but included per question requirements

## Common Pitfalls Candidates Miss

- Forgetting `restartPolicy: OnFailure` (Jobs require explicit restart policy)
- Not handling ConfigMap subPath mounting (prevents live updates)
- Missing PVC lifecycle management (orphan storage, cost accumulation)
- NetworkPolicy blocking DNS (common exam/interview mistake)
- Not considering concurrent Job execution (data corruption risk)

## Real-World Extensions

- **Argo Workflows**: For complex multi-step migrations with retry logic
- **Flyway/ Liquibase**: Tool-based migrations with built-in versioning
- **External Secrets Operator**: Dynamic credential rotation without pod restarts
- **Cilium NetworkPolicy**: More expressive than standard K8s NetworkPolicy

```yaml
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: config-migrate

spec:

          serviceAccountName: migrate-sa
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates your understanding of namespace-scoped automation, PVC usage, and secure scanning workflows within Kubernetes.

## Key Concepts
- Per-namespace CronJob with PVC mounts for manifests and logs
- Lightweight containerized scanner (e.g., trivy-lite)
- ConfigMap-based findings storage
- InitContainer for tool provisioning (jq, curl)
- Readiness and liveness probes on Job Pods
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress restrictions

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: manifest-scan
  namespace: example-ns
spec:
  schedule: "*/10 * * * *"
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 1
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          initContainers:
          - name: tools-installer
            image: busybox:1.36
            command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              wget -q https://github.com/stedolan/jq/releases/download/jq-1.6/jq-linux64 -O /tmp/jq
              chmod +x /tmp/jq
              apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
            volumeMounts:
            - name: tools
              mountPath: /tmp
          containers:
          - name: scanner
            image: trivy-lite:latest
            volumeMounts:
            - name: manifests
              mountPath: /manifests
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
            - name: tools
              mountPath: /tools
            command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              export PATH=/tmp:$PATH
              for manifest in /manifests/*.yaml; do
                trivy scan --format json -o /logs/$(basename $manifest).json $manifest
              done
              kubectl get configmap security-scan -n example-ns -o yaml > /logs/configmap-backup.yaml
            readinessProbe:
              exec:
                command:
                - ls
                - /logs
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              exec:
                command:
                - cat
                - /tmp/health
              initialDelaySeconds: 15
              periodSeconds: 20
          volumes:
          - name: manifests
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: manifest-pvc
          - name: logs
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: log-pvc
          - name: tools
            emptyDir: {}
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Trade-offs
- **PVC vs ConfigMap**: Using a PVC for logs allows for larger log volumes and retention, but requires storage provisioning. ConfigMaps are simpler but size-limited.
- **InitContainer vs Sidecar**: InitContainers run once per pod startup; sidecars run continuously. For a CronJob, InitContainers are more cost-effective.
- **NetworkPolicy**: Restricting egress improves security but may break updates if registries change. Consider using DNS whitelisting rather than specific IP ranges.
- **Probe timing**: Aggressive probes may cause premature failures; conservative settings increase job execution time.
- **CronJob frequency**: More frequent scans catch vulnerabilities faster but increase cluster load and API calls.

- InitContainer for model pull from Secret
- ConfigMap and Secret usage for runtime parameters
- Probes and HPA for reliability and scale
- Idempotent DB writes to achieve at-least-once delivery
- NetworkPolicy to enforce namespace boundaries

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ns-image-resize
  namespace: <ns>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: image-resize
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: fetch-model
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "download-model.sh"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: model
              mountPath: /models
      containers:
        - name: processor
          image: registry/ns-image-resize:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          envFrom:
            - secretRef: { name: resize-secret }
      volumes:
        - name: model
          emptyDir: {}
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
        periodSeconds: 10
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 8080
        initialDelaySeconds: 15
        periodSeconds: 20
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            - weight: 100
              podAffinityTerm:
                labelSelector:
                  matchLabels:
                    app: image-resize
                topologyKey: "kubernetes.io/hostname"
  ```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical Kubernetes hardening: securityContext at both pod and container levels, probes that reflect real app health, and a deterministic rolling update trigger. It also checks how to verify and rollback in a live system.

- PodSecurityContext and Container SecurityContext
- Probes: readiness vs liveness
- Rolling updates via PodTemplate changes (image digest annotation)

## Code Example
```yaml
# Patch sketch (showing key fields)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: worker
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        kubernetes.io/change-cause: 'security-hardening'
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
      containers:
      - name: worker
        image: your/image:tag
        securityContext:
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 80
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /readyz
            port: 80
```

## Why This Is Asked
CKAD fundamentals: volumes, InitContainers, ConfigMaps, Secrets, sidecars, network policies, and health checks in a per-namespace scope.

## Key Concepts
- Tail logs from a PVC-mounted path and write sanitized output back to the same volume
- Use a ConfigMap for PII redaction patterns
- Secure API credentials via a Secret and post summaries to an internal endpoint
- InitContainer installs tooling; sidecar rotates TLS certs
- NetworkPolicy confines egress to the internal log portal; readiness and liveness probes validate health

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal skeleton for the Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: log-redact
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: log-redact
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: log-redact
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-tools
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache sed ripgrep"]
      containers:
        - name: redactor
          image: your-registry/log-redact:latest
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
            - name: patterns
              mountPath: /patterns
          env:
            - name: POST_URL
              value: "http://logportal:8080/api/v1/sanitize"
      volumes:
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: logs-pvc
        - name: patterns
          configMap:
            name: redaction-config
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test locally with minikube?
- What failure modes require retries or idempotent postings?
